titleEn: To You I lift my eyes
progression: | Dm Gm | Dm A7 | Dm Gm | A7 Dm |
intro: Four verses, one of the fifteen Songs of Ascents, and the clearest short demonstration of how Hebrew poetry builds by repeating a root rather than by rhyming. The word for eye appears four times in the first two verses; the root for showing favour three times across verses 2 and 3; the root for having had enough twice; the word for contempt twice. Nothing in the psalm is narrated and nothing is described. The whole thing is a posture, eyes raised and held there, and the only event in it is a request. In many Ashkenazi communities the Songs of Ascents are said after Minchah on the Shabbatot between Sukkot and Passover.

stichs.en: To You I have lifted my eyes,
You who are enthroned in the heavens.

verses.summary: One person, one gesture, and an address that is a participle rather than a name. The speaker is singular here and will be plural from verse 2 to the end of the psalm.

stichs.en: Behold, like the eyes of servants toward the hand of their masters,
like the eyes of a maidservant toward the hand of her mistress,
so are our eyes toward the LORD our God, until He is gracious to us.

verses.summary: The longest verse in the psalm and the only comparison in it. Two households are set out, one male and one female, before the third clause finally says what they were being used for.

stichs.en: Be gracious to us, LORD, be gracious to us,
for we have had more than enough contempt.

verses.summary: The request, doubled, and the first time the psalm says what is wrong. Everything before this was posture; this is the petition the posture was holding.

stichs.en: Our soul has had far more than enough
of the mockery of those at ease,
of the contempt of the arrogant oppressors.

verses.summary: The complaint expanded and given owners. Contempt is not anonymous here: it belongs to people who are comfortable, and the psalm names their comfort before it names their scorn.

pardes.body: Four verses in two halves that meet on one root. Verses 1 and 2 are posture: eyes lifted to a throne, then two households in which a servant watches a hand. Verses 3 and 4 are the request and the reason for it. The hinge is {{2.17}}, until He is gracious to us, which closes the first half, and {{3.0}}, be gracious to us, which opens the second: the same root, first as a hope and then as a demand. The image in verse 2 is precise and easy to read past. Servants do not watch the master's face, they watch the hand, because the hand is where the next instruction and the next portion both come from, and the watching is continuous rather than occasional.

{{1.6}} is grammatically odd. It is the definite article plus a participle, which would ordinarily give the one who sits, but it carries an extra yod on the end that the sense does not need. The same ending turns up in a small number of poetic lines elsewhere in the Bible, and the usual account is that it preserves an old case ending kept for effect, though what it originally marked is not settled. The last two words are the hardest in the psalm. The received text divides the consonants into {{4.7}} and {{4.8}}, and that division has itself been questioned; the second element is not clearly attested anywhere else, and translations split between the proud oppressors, the arrogant, and readings that emend the consonants. The sense here is printed as the received division gives it and should be treated as disputed.

The two households of verse 2 are read as one argument made twice, and the doubling is taken as deliberate: a male servant with male masters, then a female servant with a female mistress, so that nobody hearing it can place themselves outside the comparison. The eye is the psalm's only instrument, and it is the organ that cannot act, only wait and receive, which is why there is no verb of doing anywhere in the psalm except the lifting in verse 1. Readers have also noticed that what the servant in the comparison waits for is not rescue but attention, and that the psalm never asks for the contempt to stop. It asks for favour, and favour is what a hand gives when it owes nothing.

The psalm is built on the smallest possible movement, eyes going up, and it gives that movement a destination in the first verse and then stays there for the remaining three. In the kabbalistic reading the raised eye is a standard image for a vessel turned toward its source, and the hand-watching of verse 2 is the same idea in daylight: the flow is constant and what varies is whether anyone is looking. The doubled request of {{3.0}} and {{3.2}} is read as two different askings, one for the favour and one for the capacity to hold it, which is why the verse repeats a word instead of adding one. The psalm ends on the word for the arrogant, so nothing is resolved inside the text. The resolution is the looking.
